chemicals.name: Based on the provided sources, walnuts do not contain a specific chemical "poison" or toxin

chemicals.concentration_notes: or potency: The provided sources do not specify an exact toxic dose or threshold for walnuts. They simply note that walnuts contain "high amounts" of oils and fats, which are sufficient to make a cat unwell if ingested.
chemicals.description: Cats are obligate carnivores with digestive systems that are not well-adapted to processing high amounts of plant-based oils and fats. Ingesting the high fat content found in walnuts causes gastrointestinal upset and can specifically trigger pancreatitis, which is a severe, painful, and potentially life-threatening inflammation of the pancreas.
chemicals.name: Oils and Fats (Lipids)

description: Walnuts (Juglans spp.) are not classified as chemically toxic to cats — the ASPCA lists black walnut as non-toxic to cats and its toxic principle as unknown — but they are a hazardous food that cats should not eat. The real dangers are physical and dietary rather than from a plant poison. Whole walnuts, large pieces, or hard, brittle shell fragments can cause choking or a dangerous intestinal obstruction, which may become life-threatening. The high oil and fat content is poorly digested by obligate carnivores and can cause vomiting, diarrhea, and other gastrointestinal upset, and may trigger pancreatitis (painful inflammation of the pancreas). Separately, moldy walnuts can harbor tremorgenic mycotoxins (such as Penitrem A from Penicillium mold); these are documented mainly in dogs but can cause severe tremors, ataxia, and seizures within hours of ingestion. Earlier claims that juglone is the primary feline toxin are not supported by authorities, so the practical message is: walnuts are not safe to feed, and a cat that eats a moldy walnut or shows tremors needs urgent veterinary care.
emergencyNote: Because walnuts do not contain a specific chemical poison and are instead dangerous due to their physical properties and high fat content, there is no specific chemical antidote. Instead
name: Walnuts
safetyNotes: Not chemically toxic, but not safe to feed: the ASPCA lists black walnut as non-toxic to cats with an unknown toxic principle; juglone is not an authority-supported feline toxin. Walnuts are a hazardous food, not a poison
Mycotoxin risk: mouldy walnuts can harbour tremorgenic mycotoxins (e.g. Penitrem A) — documented mainly in dogs but can cause severe tremors, ataxia, and seizures within hours
Physical hazard: walnut shells are hard and brittle; sharp fragments can injure the mouth and GI tract
High fat content: large amounts may trigger pancreatitis
If your cat ingests a mouldy walnut or shows tremors after contact with walnuts, seek veterinary care immediately

symptoms.name: If a cat ingests walnuts, the primary risks arise from the physical properties of the nut and its high fat and fiber content
Gastrointestinal Upset
symptoms.notes: The high fiber content and heavy amount of oils in nuts make them very difficult for cats to digest, easily leading to acute digestive distress.
symptoms.onset: Within a few hours of ingestion.

symptoms.name: Pancreatitis
symptoms.notes: Walnuts contain very high amounts of oils and fats, which can trigger a painful inflammation of the pancreas known as pancreatitis.
symptoms.onset: 24 to 72 hours (or progressively over a few days).

symptoms.name: Choking or Intestinal Obstruction
symptoms.notes: Because nuts are hard and difficult for a cat to digest, intact walnuts or large pieces pose a significant physical hazard. They can become lodged in the throat as a choking hazard or cause dangerous physical blockages within the intestinal tract.
symptoms.onset: Immediate (for choking) or progressive over hours to days (for intestinal blockage).

treatments.name: Because walnuts do not contain a specific chemical poison and are instead dangerous due to their physical properties and high fat content, there is no specific chemical antidote. Instead

treatments.description: of the procedure: If an intact walnut or a large, hard piece becomes lodged in the cat's throat or digestive tract, the veterinarian will need to physically remove the blockage. Depending on the location, this may involve emergency airway clearance, endoscopy, or abdominal surgery.
treatments.name: Relief of Choking or Intestinal Obstruction
treatments.notes: This is the most urgent intervention. Because walnuts are hard and difficult for cats to digest, they pose an immediate choking hazard and a high risk for intestinal blockages.

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the cat develops acute pancreatitis, they will likely require hospitalization. The veterinarian will administer intravenous (IV) fluids to combat dehydration and correct electrolyte imbalances. They will also prescribe anti-nausea medications (such as maropitant) to stop vomiting and specific pain medications (such as the opioid buprenorphine) to relieve abdominal pain.
treatments.name: Intensive Medical Management for Pancreatitis
treatments.notes: Walnuts contain very high amounts of fat, which can trigger a painful and potentially life-threatening inflammation of the pancreas (pancreatitis).

treatments.description: of the procedure: For mild to moderate cases where the walnut has passed safely but caused stomach irritation, the vet may administer subcutaneous fluids (under the skin) for hydration, prescribe anti-nausea medications, and recommend feeding a highly digestible or bland diet until the inflammation subsides.
treatments.name: Symptomatic Gastrointestinal Support
treatments.notes: The high fiber content and dense oils in nuts make them very difficult for cats to digest, commonly leading to standard stomach upset, indigestion, and diarrhea even if pancreatitis does not develop.
